source_refs.note: Angular Displacement: a main subheading of 3.1 Angular measurements, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 54-54.

blocks.text: Consider the motion of a single particle P of mass m in a circular path of radius r. Suppose this motion is taking place by attaching the particle P at the end of a massless rigid rod of length r whose other end is pivoted at the centre O of the circular path, as shown in Fig. 3.2 (a). As the particle is moving on the circular path, the rod OP rotates in the plane of the circle. The axis of rotation passes through the pivot O and is normal to the plane of rotation. Consider a system of axes as shown in Fig. 3.2 (b). The z-axis is taken along the axis of rotation with the pivot O as origin of coordinates. Axes x and y are taken in the plane of rotation. While OP is rotating, suppose at any instant t, its position is OP₁, making angle θ with x-axis. At a later time t + Δt, let its position be OP₂ making angle θ + Δθ with x-axis (Fig. 3.2-c).

blocks.alt: A circle with centre O. A rod of length r joins O to the particle P on the circle; an arrow outside the circle near P shows P moving anticlockwise.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2(a): Particle P at the end of a rod OP of length r moving on a circle (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2(a)).

blocks.alt: The circle of rotation drawn in perspective as an ellipse with O at its centre. Dashed axes from O: z straight up along the axis of rotation, y to the right and x towards the viewer. The rod OP of length r reaches the particle P on the circle.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2(b): Axes for the rotation: z along the axis of rotation through O, x and y in the plane of rotation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2(b)).

blocks.alt: A circle with centre O, a dashed x-axis to the right and a dashed y-axis upward. Two arrows of length r from O: OP₁ at angle θ to the x-axis and OP₂ a little further round, at θ + Δθ. The small angle between them is marked Δθ, and a short arrow on the circle runs from P₁ to P₂.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2(c): Position OP₁ at angle θ and, a time Δt later, OP₂ at θ + Δθ (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2(c)).

blocks.text: Angle Δθ defines the angular displacement of OP during the time interval Δt. For very small values of Δθ, the angular displacement is a vector quantity.
bold: Angle Δθ defines the angular displacement of OP during the time interval Δt. For very small values of Δθ, the angular displacement is a vector quantity.

blocks.text: The angular displacement Δθ is assigned a positive sign when the sense of rotation of OP is counter clock wise.

blocks.alt: A vertical axis of rotation passes through the centre O of a horizontal circle drawn as an ellipse. The rod OP turns anticlockwise as seen from above, shown by an arrow near P. Above the circle a right hand grasps the axis with the fingers curled in the sense of rotation and the thumb pointing up along the axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2(d): Right-hand rule for the direction of angular displacement (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.2(d)).

blocks.text: The direction associated with Δθ is along the axis of rotation and is given by right hand rule as shown in Fig 3.2 (d) which states that:
Grasp the axis of rotation in right hand with fingers curling in the direction of rotation; the thumb points in the direction of angular displacement.
bold: Grasp the axis of rotation in right hand with fingers curling in the direction of rotation; the thumb points in the direction of angular displacement.

blocks.text: Three units are generally used to express angular displacement, namely degrees, revolution and radian. Consider an arc of length S of a circle of radius r (Fig. 3.3) which subtends an angle θ at the centre of the circle. Its value in radians (rad) is given as:

blocks.text_alt: or S = rθ (where θ is in radian) ..... (3.1)

blocks.text: If OP is rotating, the point P covers a distance S = 2πr in one revolution of P. In radian, it would be:

blocks.alt: A circle with centre O and radius OP = r along the horizontal. A second radius OP₁ makes angle θ with OP. The arc from P to P₁ is drawn darker and labelled S.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: An arc PP₁ of length S subtends an angle θ at the centre O of a circle of radius r (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.3).
